newsitem.title: USA: Albright plays down Russian anti-NATO talk.
newsitem.headline: Albright plays down Russian anti-NATO talk.

text.p: New Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Thursday played down Moscow's increasingly harsh anti-NATO rhetoric and said she does not think most Russian people and the "responsible" leaders feel that way.

Interviewed by Reuters before her first overseas trip since taking office on Jan. 23, she said she would try to persuade Russian leaders during talks in Moscow on Feb. 20-21 "not to see NATO as an adversarial alliance against Russia."

Other U.S. officials told Reuters Albright was expected to outline for Russian leaders during her visit details of a new conventional arms reduction proposal being developed by NATO as a means of assuring Moscow about the non-threatening nature of an enlarged western alliance.

Officials said she might also brief Moscow on a new but as yet unpublished State Department-Pentagon study on the projected costs of expanding NATO and the assumptions and perceived threats underlying those calculations.

Officials said the bottom line expansion costs are less than a controversial study issued by the Rand Corp last year. The Rand study said the costs could range from $10 billion and to $110 billion but likely would be in the $30 billion to $52 billion range over a 10-15 year period.

The alliance plans to decide at a summit in July on which new members to admit. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary are top contenders. Romania and Slovenia are also discussed but U.S. officials tend to doubt they will be accepted in the first post-Cold War expansion round.

In an effort to assuage Russian concerns about its plans to absorb former Soviet bloc states, NATO has proposed a charter with Russia defining a special relationship between the alliance and Moscow. Although talks have begun, Russia remains vigorously opposed to NATO expansion.

In a fresh burst of rhetorical gunfire, the Kremlin on Wednesday accused NATO and its Secretary-General Javier Solana of pursuing a covert anti-Moscow policy, prompting swift denials by the alliance and raising new tensions.

Moscow's campaign had reached a new peak a day earlier when one official said Russia should be ready to use nuclear weapons if subjected to a conventional arms attack, although the Kremlin later distanced itself from those comments.

Asked why the rhetoric was worsening despite a vigorous U.S. and allied defence of NATO expansion, Albright said: "I don't buy into that. I think the important part here is that from what we know ... the people of Russia don't see it that way, nor does the responsible leadership."
She cautioned against a downward spiral of attacks over NATO and said she hoped to help the Russians understand "the overriding importance of a good U.S.-Russian relationship."
"It's very important for people not to have old think about NATO and about the direction in which we want to go."

"Generally people need to not see NATO as an adversarial alliance against Russia but basically a way that the institutions of Europe can be strengthened in a security system that is not opposed to somebody," Albright said.
Another senior official told Reuters the harsher rhetoric was consistent with Russia's strong opposition to enlargement and the fact that the crucial NATO summit is fast approaching.
But he said there are "contradictory elements in what the Russian are saying ... I think it is indicative of the fact that this is a very confused and confusing issue for the Russian government."

He said Washington takes its cue from "authoritative" Russians like Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin who made clear in a visit here this week that while Russia deeply opposes NATO enlargement the Kremlin wants to develop a set of cooperative understandings between Moscow and the alliance.
In an article in Britain's Economist magazine this week, Albright said the administration had "no higher priority" than to enlarge NATO by 1999.
